topics.name: Refraction
topics.kicker: Bending of a wave entering a new material · Why straws look broken
topics.briefing: Refraction is the bending that happens when a wave like light slows down or speeds up while crossing from one material into another, such as air into water. It is why a straw in a glass of water looks snapped in two and why a prism spreads white light into a rainbow. Snell’s law, a rule connecting the bending angle to a fixed number for each material, describes exactly how much a wave bends.

trap.title: Refraction, or reflection/diffraction?
trap.body: All three are things a wave can do at a boundary, and real tossups are strict about which one they want: a real refraction answer line explicitly says “do not accept reflection or diffraction,” while real reflection and diffraction tossups explicitly reject “refraction” right back. Reflection is light bouncing off a surface and staying in the same material; diffraction is a wave bending around obstacles or spreading out after a narrow slit, tested with the Davisson-Germer experiment and Bragg’s law.
trap.fix: If the clues describe a wave crossing into a new material and changing speed (Snell’s law, a bent straw, a lens), it is refraction. If a mirror or “angle of incidence equals angle of reflection” shows up, it is reflection. If slits, gratings, or spreading around an edge shows up, it is diffraction.

topics.name: Electrons
topics.kicker: Negatively charged particles around the nucleus · They carry electric current
topics.briefing: Electrons are tiny, negatively charged particles that swarm around the nucleus of every atom, vastly outweighed in mass by the protons and neutrons packed inside it. J. J. Thomson discovered them in 1897 using a cathode ray tube, proving that atoms are not solid, indivisible balls after all. The outermost ones are what atoms trade or share to form chemical bonds, and their steady flow through a wire is what we call electric current.

trap.title: Leptons, not quarks
trap.body: These particles are fundamental leptons that are not built from anything smaller. The protons and neutrons they orbit, by contrast, are each built from three even tinier quarks, a completely different family. A kid who mixes up the two families might blurt “quark” for a particle clue about the nucleus, or blurt this particle’s name for a clue that is really describing the quarks hiding inside a proton.
trap.fix: If the clue describes something negatively charged orbiting the nucleus, discovered by J. J. Thomson, or traded in chemical bonds, it is this particle. If the clue describes “up” and “down” types combining in threes to build protons and neutrons, that is quarks instead.

topics.name: Pressure
topics.kicker: Force spread over an area · Measured by barometers, keeps airplanes aloft
topics.dates: SI unit: the pascal, named for Blaise Pascal
topics.briefing: Pressure is simply how much force pushes on every bit of a surface’s area, whether that is air pressing on your body, water squeezing a submarine, or gas rattling around inside a tire. Scientists measure it in pascals, and everyday tools like barometers and manometers track it using a column of liquid such as mercury. Pascal’s principle explains why squeezing one part of an enclosed fluid, as in hydraulic brakes, pushes evenly throughout the whole thing.

topics.name: Energy
topics.kicker: The capacity to do work · Shifts between forms but is never lost
topics.briefing: Energy is the capacity to move something, heat it up, light it up, or change it in any way, and physicists measure it in joules. It never appears from nothing and never disappears — the law of conservation says it only converts between forms, like a falling apple trading stored height for speed. Albert Einstein even showed that mass itself is a tightly packed form of it.

tossups.p: Combining time symmetry with a theorem from Emmy Noether proves that the total amount of this quantity in an isolated system cannot change, which is why machines that run forever without fuel are impossible. For such a system, the overall value of this quantity is given by a function called the Hamiltonian.
tossups.r: This quantity is stored inside a capacitor’s electric field. Its SI unit describes the work done when a force of one newton moves something one meter. For 10 points, name this physical quantity, measured in joules, which comes in forms tied to motion and to stored position.

tossups.p: For a single particle of light, this quantity equals Planck’s constant multiplied by the light’s frequency. Albert Einstein’s most famous equation relates this quantity to an object’s mass, multiplying it by the speed of light squared.
tossups.r: Food Calories on a nutrition label are really a unit of this quantity. Work measures the transfer of this quantity. For 10 points, name this quantity that is measured in joules and comes in forms tied to motion and to stored height or position.

tossups.p: A capacitor stores this quantity inside the electric field between its two plates. Because this quantity is always conserved, so-called perpetual motion machines, which would run forever without any outside fuel, can never actually work.
tossups.r: Snapping a glow stick starts a chemical reaction that releases this quantity as light instead of heat. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in joules, which is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

tossups.p: This quantity’s SI unit equals the work done by a one-newton force acting over one meter. Splitting a heavy atomic nucleus apart, or fusing two light ones together, both release huge amounts of this quantity.
tossups.r: Wind turbines, solar panels, and dams all turn naturally renewable sources into a usable form of this quantity, unlike burning coal, oil, or natural gas. For 10 points, name this quantity that a moving object has in one form and a raised or stretched object stores in another.

Electric companies bill customers in kilowatt-hours, a unit of this quantity equal to running a thousand-watt device for one hour.

tossups.r: A battery converts a stored chemical form of this quantity into an electrical form that can light a bulb. For 10 points, name this quantity that is conserved overall even as it keeps changing from one form into another.

tossups.p: This quantity is stored in the electric field of a charged capacitor and can also be carried by a single photon in an amount equal to Planck’s constant times frequency. A device that claimed to produce more of this quantity than it consumes, forever, would violate its own conservation law.
tossups.r: Muscles convert a stored chemical form of this quantity, originally from food, into the kind linked to motion. For 10 points, name this quantity, whose SI unit, the joule, honors English physicist James Prescott Joule.

tossups.r: A plant’s leaves capture sunlight and lock this quantity away in chemical form inside sugar molecules. For 10 points, name this quantity, which a stretched spring stores in one form and a speeding car carries in another.

tossups.p: Combining time symmetry with Noether’s theorem shows that the total amount of this quantity never changes in an isolated system, which is why no machine can run forever without fuel. A single photon of light carries an amount of this quantity set by its frequency and Planck’s constant.
tossups.r: A toaster converts an electrical form of this quantity into heat and light. For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in joules, that comes in a form tied to an object’s motion and a form tied to its stored position or condition.

tossups.r: A car battery stores a chemical form of this quantity that becomes electrical to start the engine. For 10 points, name this quantity whose moving form equals one-half mass times velocity squared.

tossups.p: Earth’s internal heat and the Moon’s gravitational pull on the oceans both supply renewable, naturally replenished sources of this quantity, geothermal and tidal. This quantity’s SI unit equals the work a one-newton force does moving something one meter.
tossups.r: Burning natural gas releases a stored chemical form of this quantity as heat and light. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is measured on food packaging in Calories and physically in joules.

tossups.p: An object’s mass is, according to Einstein, an extremely concentrated form of this quantity, related by the speed of light squared. This quantity trapped between the plates of a charged capacitor can later be released as an electric current.
tossups.r: A roller coaster car at the top of a hill stores a form of this quantity based on height, which converts into a moving form as it speeds downward. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in joules.

topics.name: Entropy
topics.kicker: Measure of disorder · Never decreases in an isolated system
topics.briefing: Entropy measures disorder: how many different ways the tiny particles in a system can be arranged. It explains why ice melts in a warm room and why a dropped egg never puts itself back together, because in an isolated system, entropy never goes down. Rudolf Clausius named it in 1865, and Ludwig Boltzmann’s formula for it, S = k log W, is carved on his tombstone in Vienna.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ludwig Boltzmann’s [“BOHLTS-mahnz”] tombstone in Vienna is carved with a formula for this quantity: a constant k times the logarithm of W, the number of tiny arrangements a system’s particles can have. For a reversible process, a change in this quantity equals the heat added divided by the absolute temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of a system’s disorder, which never decreases in an isolated system.

tossups.p: Rudolf Clausius [“KLOW-zee-us”] coined this quantity’s name in 1865 from a Greek word for “transformation,” choosing it to sound like the word “energy.” Clausius summed up thermodynamics by saying that the energy of the universe is constant, while this quantity tends toward a maximum.
tossups.r: It is measured in joules per kelvin. For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized S, often described as a measure of disorder.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny “demon” that guards a door between two boxes of gas, letting fast molecules through one way and slow ones the other. By sorting the molecules without doing any work, that demon would seem to lower this quantity.
tossups.r: A reaction that makes more gas molecules than it uses up usually increases it. For 10 points, name this quantity that the second law of thermodynamics says never decreases in an isolated system.

tossups.p: Jacob Bekenstein [“BEK-en-stine”] proposed that a black hole has an amount of this quantity proportional to the area of its event horizon, an idea supported when Stephen Hawking showed that black holes give off radiation.
tossups.r: A substance’s gas form has more of this quantity than its liquid or solid forms. For 10 points, name this measure of disorder.

tossups.p: In 1948, Claude Shannon defined a version of this quantity that measures the average information in a message, counted in bits. The total change in this quantity for an engine and its surroundings is zero for a perfectly reversible cycle, but positive for any real engine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that measures disorder, which the second law of thermodynamics says tends to increase.

tossups.p: Linus Pauling explained why ordinary ice keeps a leftover amount of this quantity even close to absolute zero: its hydrogen atoms can be arranged in a huge number of ways. The third law of thermodynamics says that this quantity is zero for a perfect crystal at absolute zero.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized S, which increases when ice melts into liquid water.

tossups.p: On a graph of temperature versus this quantity, a Carnot [“kar-NOH”] cycle forms a rectangle, since its two reversible adiabatic steps leave this quantity unchanged. The area enclosed by a cycle on that kind of graph equals the net work the engine does.
tossups.r: Heat flowing from a hot object to a cold one increases this quantity. For 10 points, name this measure of disorder, symbolized S.

tossups.p: Chemists predict whether a reaction will happen on its own by multiplying this quantity by temperature and subtracting the result from the enthalpy, giving the Gibbs free energy. A reaction that releases heat and also increases this quantity is spontaneous at every temperature.
tossups.r: Melting ice and boiling water both increase this quantity. For 10 points, name this measure of disorder, symbolized S.

tossups.p: Arthur Eddington coined the phrase “arrow of time” for the one-way direction that the steady rise of this quantity seems to give the universe. This quantity explains why a shattered glass never jumps back together, even though the laws of motion work the same forward and backward.
tossups.r: The second law of thermodynamics says this quantity never decreases in an isolated system. For 10 points, name this measure of disorder, symbolized S.

tossups.p: In a possible far-future “heat death,” this quantity would reach its maximum value for the whole universe, leaving no temperature differences to power anything. A change in this quantity can be found by dividing the heat added in a reversible process by the absolute temperature.
tossups.r: Ice melting in a warm room increases it. For 10 points, name this measure of disorder, which never decreases in an isolated system.

tossups.p: Removing a wall between two different gases so that they mix raises this quantity, even when both gases start at the same temperature and pressure. Ludwig Boltzmann explained this quantity by counting the number of ways a system’s particles can be arranged.
tossups.r: The total amount of this quantity rises whenever heat flows from a hot object to a cold one. For 10 points, name this measure of disorder, symbolized S.

tossups.p: When an ideal gas expands freely into a vacuum, no heat flows in and its temperature stays the same, yet this quantity still increases. This quantity is a state function, so its change depends only on a system’s starting and ending states, not on the path between them.
tossups.r: The second law of thermodynamics says this quantity never decreases in an isolated system. For 10 points, name this measure of disorder.

tossups.p: Erwin Schrödinger’s [“SHROH-ding-erz”] 1944 book _What Is Life?_ argued that living things stay alive by “feeding on” the negative of this quantity. A living cell can lower this quantity inside itself only by raising it even more in its surroundings, for example by giving off heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of disorder, which the second law of thermodynamics says tends to increase.

tossups.p: Walther Nernst’s heat theorem, which grew into the third law of thermodynamics, says that the change in this quantity during a chemical reaction shrinks toward zero as the temperature nears absolute zero. When a liquid boils at a steady temperature, the change in this quantity equals the heat it absorbs divided by that temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of disorder, symbolized S, which the second law of thermodynamics says never decreases in an isolated system.

tossups.p: The Clausius [“KLOW-zee-us”] inequality leads to the rule that, in any real process, the change in this quantity is greater than the heat added divided by the temperature. This quantity, measured in joules per kelvin, has the same units as the Boltzmann constant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that increases when ice melts, often described as a measure of disorder.

trap.title: Entropy, not enthalpy
trap.body: Entropy (S, disorder) and enthalpy (H, heat content) sound alike and sit side by side in the Gibbs free energy equation, G = H − TS, so players mix them up. Players also blurt “second law of thermodynamics” when the question wants the quantity that law is about.
trap.fix: Disorder, Boltzmann’s S = k log W, “joules per kelvin,” and anything that “never decreases” point to entropy. Heat content, heats of reaction, and Hess’s law point to enthalpy. If the question asks for “this quantity,” name the quantity, not the law.

topics.name: Doppler effect
topics.kicker: Wave shift from a moving source · Why passing sirens drop in pitch
topics.briefing: Stand by the road as an ambulance races past, and its siren suddenly drops from a high pitch to a low one: that is the Doppler effect. Waves bunch up in front of a moving source and stretch out behind it, so the frequency you hear changes. Austrian physicist Christian Doppler described it in 1842, and astronomers use the same effect in light to tell whether stars are moving toward us or away.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1845, the Dutch scientist Christophorus Buys Ballot tested this effect using musicians who played a steady note while riding on a train near Utrecht, as listeners with perfect pitch stood beside the tracks. This effect’s namesake had proposed it three years earlier.
tossups.r: This effect makes an ambulance siren sound higher as it approaches and lower as it speeds away. For 10 points, name this change in a wave’s frequency caused by motion.

tossups.p: Hippolyte Fizeau [“fee-ZOH”] independently worked out the version of this effect for light in 1848, so the French often add his name to it. Light from a star moving away from us is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum by this effect.
tossups.r: Its Austrian namesake first described it in 1842. For 10 points, name this effect that makes a passing train’s horn drop in pitch.

tossups.p: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz [“kuh-LOH”] shared a Nobel Prize for finding the planet 51 Pegasi b in 1995 by using this effect to detect a star wobbling back and forth. That radial velocity method looks for a star’s spectral lines shifting slightly toward red and then toward blue.
tossups.r: Police radar guns use it to measure the speed of cars. For 10 points, name this effect that makes an approaching siren sound higher in pitch.

tossups.p: This effect’s namesake, a physicist born in Salzburg, later taught physics at the University of Vienna, where his students included the future “father of genetics,” Gregor Mendel. A star’s spectral lines move toward the blue end of the spectrum because of this effect when the star approaches Earth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which the motion of a wave’s source changes the frequency an observer detects.

tossups.p: Steven Chu shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics for cooling atoms with lasers tuned slightly below an atom’s natural frequency, a technique named for this effect. Atoms moving toward such a laser see its light shifted up to just the right frequency to absorb it, which slows them down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that makes a race car’s engine sound drop in pitch as the car zooms past.

tossups.p: Thermal motion of the atoms in a gas widens their spectral lines through a broadening named for this effect, so the width of a line can reveal the gas’s temperature. This effect explains why a star’s spectral lines shift back and forth as it orbits a companion in a spectroscopic binary.
tossups.r: An Austrian physicist described it in 1842. For 10 points, name this effect that makes a passing siren drop in pitch.

tossups.p: A Leslie speaker, often paired with a Hammond organ, spins its horn in a circle so that this effect makes the sound wobble in pitch. This effect happens because waves in front of a moving source are bunched closer together, while waves behind it are stretched out.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that makes a moving car’s horn sound higher as it approaches you.

tossups.p: Scientists at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory worked out the orbit of Sputnik 1 in 1957 by tracking how this effect shifted the frequency of its radio signal as it passed overhead, work that led to the Transit satellite navigation system.
tossups.r: Police radar guns use this effect to measure the speed of cars. For 10 points, name this effect that causes a passing ambulance’s siren to drop in pitch.

tossups.p: This effect’s Austrian namesake wrongly suggested in an 1842 paper that it explained the different colors of double stars, which actually come from their temperatures. Weather radars use this effect to spot winds rotating inside thunderstorms that may produce tornadoes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that makes a siren sound higher as it approaches and lower as it moves away.

tossups.p: Starting in 1912, Vesto Slipher [“SLY-fer”] used this effect to measure how fast spiral nebulae were moving, finding that most of them were rushing away from us. Edwin Hubble later combined those speeds with distances to find that farther galaxies are moving away faster.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that makes a train whistle drop in pitch as the train passes.

tossups.p: Light from the Andromeda Galaxy is shifted toward the blue end of the spectrum by this effect, showing that Andromeda is moving toward the Milky Way. The frequency an observer detects in this effect depends on how fast the source and observer move compared with the wave.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that makes an ambulance’s siren sound higher-pitched as it comes closer.

tossups.p: Doctors use ultrasound machines that rely on this effect to measure how fast blood is flowing through the heart and arteries. This effect does not change the speed of the sound waves; it changes how many wave crests reach a listener each second.
tossups.r: It shifts the spectral lines of stars moving away from Earth toward red. For 10 points, name this effect that makes a passing siren drop in pitch.

tossups.p: If a source of sound moves toward you at half the speed of sound, this effect doubles the frequency you hear. Only the part of the motion directly toward or away from the listener matters in the everyday form of this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that makes an ambulance siren sound higher as it approaches.

tossups.p: Astronomers can measure how fast the Sun rotates by comparing light from its two edges, since this effect shifts light from the edge turning toward us toward blue and light from the other edge toward red.
tossups.r: Radar guns use it to clock tennis serves. For 10 points, name this effect that makes a passing train’s whistle drop in pitch.

tossups.p: A driver passing a ringing railroad-crossing bell hears its pitch drop, an example of this effect in which the listener, not the source, is moving. Water waves from a duck paddling across a pond bunch up in front of it and spread apart behind it, showing this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect named for an Austrian physicist, heard when a fire truck’s siren drops in pitch as it passes.

trap.title: Shift, not sonic boom
trap.body: A sonic boom happens when a jet outruns its own sound waves; it is related, but it is not this effect. Redshift and blueshift are results of this effect in light, so saying just “redshift” may only earn a prompt. And “frequency” names the thing that changes, not the effect itself.
trap.fix: When the clues describe a pitch or a color that changes because something is moving toward or away from you, say “Doppler effect.” Shock waves and breaking the sound barrier mean sonic boom.

topics.name: Angular momentum
topics.kicker: Rotation’s conserved quantity · Why skaters spin faster with arms in
topics.dates: Kepler’s second law (1609) reflects its conservation
topics.briefing: Angular momentum is the spinning version of momentum: it grows with an object’s mass, with how far that mass sits from the center, and with how fast the object turns. When no outside twist, or torque, acts on a system, its angular momentum stays the same, which is why a figure skater spins faster when she pulls in her arms. The same rule makes collapsing stars spin up and helps a spinning top stay upright.
topics.answerHtml: Angular momentum (prompt on L or momentum; do not accept “linear momentum”)
accept: law of conservation of angular momentum

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Emmy Noether’s [“NUR-terz”] theorem links the conservation of this quantity to the fact that the laws of physics work the same no matter which direction a system faces. The net torque on an object equals the rate at which this quantity changes over time.
tossups.r: A figure skater who pulls in her arms spins faster because this quantity is conserved. For 10 points, name this rotational quantity, equal to moment of inertia times angular velocity.

tossups.p: In his 1913 model of the hydrogen atom, Niels Bohr assumed that the electron’s value of this quantity in each allowed orbit is a whole-number multiple of Planck’s constant divided by two pi. This quantity is a vector that points along the axis of rotation, following the right-hand rule.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that a spinning object keeps constant unless an outside torque acts on it.

tossups.p: In 1922, Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach [“GAIR-lahk”] sent silver atoms through an uneven magnetic field and saw the beam split in two, showing that this quantity can only line up in certain directions. The built-in form of this quantity carried by an electron is called spin.
tossups.r: Gymnasts tuck their bodies to flip faster because this quantity is conserved. For 10 points, name this rotational quantity, symbolized L.

tossups.p: Kepler’s second law, which says a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, is really a consequence of the conservation of this quantity. Because this quantity stays fixed, a comet moves fastest when it swings closest to the Sun.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which equals moment of inertia times angular velocity and is symbolized L.

tossups.p: Tides slowly transfer this quantity from Earth’s spin to the Moon’s orbit, which is why Earth’s days are getting longer and the Moon drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther away each year. A spinning top or gyroscope resists tipping over because of this quantity.
tossups.r: Ice skaters spin faster when they pull in their arms because it is conserved. For 10 points, name this rotational quantity, symbolized L.

tossups.p: The Sun holds more than 99 percent of the Solar System’s mass but only a tiny share of this quantity, most of which is carried by Jupiter’s orbit. A cloud of gas collapsing to form a star spins faster and flattens into a disk because this quantity is conserved.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational quantity, symbolized L, that equals moment of inertia times angular velocity.

tossups.p: When a giant star’s core collapses into a neutron star only about 20 kilometers across, conservation of this quantity can make the tiny star spin many times per second. A diver who tucks into a ball flips faster for the same reason.
tossups.r: It is symbolized L. For 10 points, name this quantity, the product of moment of inertia and angular velocity.

tossups.p: This quantity has the same units as Planck’s constant, joule-seconds, which can also be written as kilogram meters squared per second. For a point mass, this quantity equals the cross product of its position vector with its mass times velocity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that explains why ice skaters spin faster when they pull in their arms.

tossups.p: The azimuthal quantum number, written as a lowercase l, sets the size of an electron’s orbital value of this quantity and decides whether its orbital is s, p, d, or f. A helicopter needs a tail rotor because its body would otherwise spin opposite the main rotor to conserve this quantity.
tossups.r: Figure skaters spin faster by pulling in their arms because it is conserved. For 10 points, name this rotational quantity, symbolized L.

tossups.p: A child who walks from the middle of a freely spinning merry-go-round out to its edge makes it turn more slowly, because this quantity stays the same. A person sitting on a swivel stool who flips over a spinning bicycle wheel starts turning because this quantity is conserved.
tossups.r: It is symbolized L. For 10 points, name this rotational quantity, equal to moment of inertia times angular velocity.

tossups.p: Gravity’s torque on a tilted spinning top changes the direction of this quantity instead of knocking the top over, so the top’s axis slowly circles in a motion called precession. A football thrown in a tight spiral flies steadily because of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized L, that a figure skater conserves while spinning.

tossups.p: A falling cat can twist around to land on its feet even though its total of this quantity stays zero, by changing its body’s shape. A spacecraft can turn itself by spinning a reaction wheel the opposite way, since the total of this quantity must stay the same.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational quantity, symbolized L, that stays constant when no outside torque acts on a system.

tossups.p: In the Einstein–de Haas effect, magnetizing a hanging iron cylinder makes it start to rotate, showing that the magnetism of electrons is tied to this quantity. Electrons carry a built-in form of this quantity called spin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose conservation explains Kepler’s second law and why spinning skaters speed up.

tossups.p: Multiplying the torque on an object by the time it acts gives the change in this quantity. Earth moves fastest in its orbit in early January, when it is closest to the Sun, because this quantity stays the same.
tossups.r: For a rigid body, it equals the moment of inertia times the angular velocity. For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized L, whose conservation makes a figure skater spin faster.

tossups.p: The no-hair theorem says a black hole can be described completely by just three numbers: its mass, its electric charge, and this quantity. A rotating Kerr black hole has some of this quantity, while a Schwarzschild [“SHVARTS-shilt”] black hole has none.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized L, which a spinning ice skater conserves.

clues.t: A figure skater spins faster when she pulls in her arms, because it stays constant
Equals moment of inertia (I) times angular velocity (omega): L = Iω
Symbolized L; the rotational counterpart of mass times velocity
Conserved whenever no net outside torque acts on a system
Net torque equals its rate of change over time
Its conservation explains Kepler’s second law (equal areas in equal times), so a comet moves fastest near the Sun
A collapsing star core becomes a fast-spinning neutron star (pulsar) because it is conserved
A vector pointing along the axis of rotation, found with the right-hand rule
Keeps spinning tops and gyroscopes from tipping; gravity’s torque makes them precess instead
For a point mass, the cross product of position and mass times velocity: L = r × p
Divers and gymnasts tuck into a ball to flip faster
A helicopter’s tail rotor keeps the body from spinning opposite the main rotor
Flipping a spinning bicycle wheel while sitting on a swivel stool makes you start turning
Emmy Noether’s theorem: its conservation comes from the laws of physics being the same in every direction
Niels Bohr’s 1913 model: an electron’s value is a whole-number multiple of h-bar (Planck’s constant over 2π)
Stern–Gerlach experiment (1922): a beam of silver atoms split in two, showing it can only line up in certain directions
Measured in joule-seconds (kilogram meters squared per second), the same units as Planck’s constant
Spin is the built-in (intrinsic) form carried by particles such as electrons
Tides move it from Earth’s spin to the Moon’s orbit: days get longer and the Moon drifts about 3.8 cm farther away each year
The Sun has over 99% of the Solar System’s mass but little of this; Jupiter’s orbit carries most of it
The azimuthal quantum number l sets an electron’s orbital value and whether the orbital is s, p, d, or f
A child walking from the middle of a spinning merry-go-round out to its edge makes it turn more slowly
A falling cat rights itself with a total of zero by changing its body’s shape
Spacecraft turn by spinning reaction wheels the opposite way
Einstein–de Haas effect: magnetizing a hanging iron cylinder makes it rotate
No-hair theorem: a black hole is described by its mass, charge, and this; Kerr black holes have some, Schwarzschild ones none
Torque multiplied by the time it acts gives its change, called angular impulse

trap.title: Angular, not linear
trap.body: Angular momentum (the spinning kind) and plain momentum (mass times velocity) are separate answer lines, and torque and moment of inertia show up in the same formulas. Saying just “momentum” only earns a prompt, so say the whole answer, “angular momentum.” Noether’s theorem trips people up too: rotation symmetry gives angular momentum, while sameness everywhere in space gives ordinary momentum.
trap.fix: Spinning, orbiting, skaters pulling in their arms, Kepler’s equal areas, L, Iω, and h-bar mean angular momentum. Collisions, p = mv, impulse, and rockets mean ordinary (linear) momentum. A twisting force is torque; resistance to starting a spin is moment of inertia.
trap.line: Real answer line: Angular momentum (prompt on L or momentum; do not accept “linear momentum”)

topics.name: Nuclear fusion
topics.kicker: Light nuclei joining into heavier ones · The power source of the stars
topics.dates: Proposed as the Sun’s power source, 1920
topics.briefing: Nuclear fusion happens when two light atomic nuclei slam together so hard that they merge into a heavier one, turning a little of their mass into a lot of energy. It powers the Sun, which joins hydrogen nuclei into helium in a core heated to about 15 million degrees. Scientists around the world are trying to build fusion reactors that could one day make electricity from fuel found in seawater.
topics.answerHtml: nuclear fusion (prompt on nuclear reaction; do not accept “fission”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1920, Arthur Eddington proposed that this process powers the stars, using Francis Aston’s measurements showing that a helium atom weighs slightly less than four hydrogen atoms. That missing mass is turned into energy according to E equals m c squared.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which light atomic nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, as in the core of the Sun.

tossups.p: Hans Bethe [“BAY-tuh”] won the 1967 Nobel Prize for explaining how stars make energy, including a cycle in which carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen nuclei act as catalysts. That CNO cycle and the proton-proton chain are two ways stars carry out this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium, releasing the energy that makes stars shine.

tossups.p: Fred Hoyle predicted that carbon-12 must have a special excited energy state, or the triple-alpha process could never produce enough carbon. In that process, which happens in red giant stars, three helium-4 nuclei join to form one carbon nucleus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this type of nuclear reaction that powers the Sun, in which small nuclei combine into a larger one.

tossups.p: John Lawson worked out a condition for this process to produce more energy than it uses, based on the product of a plasma’s density, its temperature, and how long its energy stays trapped. Reactors for this process often use deuterium and tritium, two heavy forms of hydrogen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that powers the Sun, in which light nuclei combine, the opposite of nuclear fission.

tossups.p: Igor Tamm and Andrei Sakharov [“SAH-kuh-rawf”] invented the tokamak, a doughnut-shaped machine that uses powerful magnets to hold a plasma heated to over 100 million degrees for this process. Physicists hope such machines will one day generate electricity from this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, the energy source of the Sun, in which light nuclei combine.

tossups.p: Lyman Spitzer invented the stellarator, a twisted ring-shaped machine for this process, in 1951; Germany’s giant Wendelstein [“VEN-dul-shtine”] 7-X is one of them. Like a tokamak, it uses magnetic fields to hold a plasma away from the walls of its chamber.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium inside stars.

tossups.p: In December 2022, the National Ignition Facility in California fired 192 laser beams at a tiny fuel pellet and, for the first time, got more energy out of this process than the lasers put in. That approach is called inertial confinement.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that powers the stars, in which light nuclei combine into heavier ones.

tossups.p: More than 30 countries, including the United States, China, Japan, and members of the European Union, are building a giant experimental reactor for this process at Cadarache [“kah-dah-RASH”] in southern France. That reactor, a tokamak, is called ITER, which means “the way” in Latin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that powers the Sun, in which light nuclei join.

tossups.p: Future reactors for this process may make their own tritium fuel by hitting lithium with neutrons in a “breeding blanket.” The easiest version of this process to achieve on Earth joins deuterium and tritium, producing a helium-4 nucleus and a fast neutron.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that powers the Sun, the opposite of splitting heavy nuclei in fission.

tossups.p: Quantum tunneling lets protons in the Sun’s core slip past the strong electric repulsion between them, called the Coulomb barrier, so that they can undergo this process at about 15 million kelvins.
tossups.r: In the Sun, it mostly follows the proton-proton chain. For 10 points, name this process in which hydrogen nuclei combine into helium.

tossups.p: Brown dwarfs are too small to keep up the hydrogen version of this process in their cores, though many can briefly carry it out with deuterium. A star joins the main sequence once this process begins turning hydrogen into helium in its core.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that makes stars shine, in which light nuclei combine.

tossups.p: Ray Davis used a giant tank of cleaning fluid deep in a South Dakota mine to catch neutrinos made by this process in the Sun, but he found only about a third as many as expected. That “solar neutrino problem” was solved when physicists learned that neutrinos change type.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which hydrogen nuclei combine into helium in the Sun’s core.

tossups.p: This process gives off energy only when it builds nuclei up to about the size of iron, since iron and nickel have the most tightly bound nuclei. A dying massive star that builds up an iron core can no longer make energy by this process, and the core collapses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, the opposite of fission, that powers stars by joining light nuclei together.

tossups.p: Working with Ernest Rutherford in the 1930s, Mark Oliphant carried out this process in a laboratory by smashing deuterium nuclei together, discovering helium-3 and tritium along the way. Through this process, the Sun turns about 4 million tons of its mass into energy every second.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which light nuclei combine, releasing the energy that powers stars.

tossups.p: The Teller–Ulam design used an atomic bomb to set off this process in a much more powerful weapon, first tested as “Ivy Mike” at Enewetak Atoll in 1952. That weapon is often called the hydrogen bomb.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which light nuclei join into a heavier nucleus, the reverse of fission.

Hans Bethe won the 1967 Nobel Prize for explaining how stars make energy, including the CNO cycle

trap.title: Fusion, not fission
trap.body: Fusion and fission are both nuclear reactions that release huge amounts of energy, and the two words sound alike under buzzer pressure. Fission splits heavy nuclei such as uranium and runs ordinary nuclear power plants; fusion joins light nuclei such as hydrogen and powers the Sun.
trap.fix: Think “fusion = join, fission = split.” Stars, hydrogen into helium, tokamaks, ITER, and deuterium-tritium mean fusion. Uranium, plutonium, chain reactions, and Enrico Fermi’s first reactor mean fission.
trap.line: Real answer line: nuclear fusion (prompt on nuclear reaction; do not accept “fission”)

topics.name: Viscosity
topics.kicker: A fluid’s resistance to flow · Why honey pours slower than water
topics.dates: Newton’s law for it published in 1687
topics.briefing: Viscosity is a fluid’s resistance to flowing: it is why honey oozes slowly off a spoon while water splashes right out of a glass. Most liquids get runnier as they warm up, which is why syrup pours faster after a turn in the microwave. Some strange fluids, like a cornstarch-and-water mix called oobleck, suddenly act thicker when you punch or squeeze them.
topics.answerHtml: Viscosity (accept dynamic or kinematic viscosity; prompt on thickness or internal friction)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A funnel of tar pitch set up at the University of Queensland in 1927 had let only nine drops fall by 2014, because pitch has an enormous value of this property. Thomas Parnell started that experiment to show that a substance that shatters under a hammer can still slowly flow.
tossups.r: Honey has a higher value of this property than water. For 10 points, name this property, a fluid’s resistance to flow.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell surprised scientists by predicting that this property of a gas does not depend on the gas’s pressure, and he confirmed it using disks that twisted back and forth in gas. Unlike liquids, gases have more of this property when they get hotter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that measures how strongly a fluid resists flowing, which is high for honey and molasses.

tossups.p: In 1937, Pyotr Kapitsa, and separately John Allen and Don Misener, found that liquid helium cooled below about 2.2 kelvins flows through tiny gaps with none of this property. Such a superfluid can even creep up and over the walls of its container.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that describes how “thick” a fluid is, which makes honey flow slowly.

tossups.p: Deciding whether the Navier–Stokes [“nahv-YAY STOHKS”] equations, which describe fluids that have this property, always have smooth solutions is one of the Clay Institute’s million-dollar Millennium Prize Problems. This property is the reason a stirred cup of tea eventually stops swirling.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, a fluid’s internal resistance to flow, which is much higher for honey than for water.

tossups.p: Jean Poiseuille [“pwah-ZOY”], a French doctor who studied blood flow, found that the flow through a narrow tube depends on the tube’s radius to the fourth power divided by this property. A unit of this property, the poise, is named after him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of fluids that is much higher for molasses than for water.

tossups.p: Robert Millikan used Stokes’ law, which says the drag on a small falling sphere equals six pi times this property times the sphere’s radius and speed, to find the sizes of his oil drops. Students can measure this property by timing steel balls as they sink through tubes of oil.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, measured in pascal-seconds, that describes how strongly a fluid resists flowing.

tossups.p: The Reynolds number compares a fluid’s inertia to this property, and a low Reynolds number means smooth, layered flow instead of turbulence. Osborne Reynolds studied the switch between those kinds of flow by injecting a thin stream of dye into water flowing through a glass pipe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, a fluid’s resistance to flow, which is higher for syrup than for water.

tossups.p: The Society of Automotive Engineers grades motor oils for this property using labels like 10W-30, where the W stands for “winter” and the first number describes how the oil behaves when cold.
tossups.r: Warming most liquids lowers this property. For 10 points, name this property, which is why honey pours more slowly than water.

tossups.p: A mix of cornstarch and water called oobleck, named after the Dr. Seuss book _Bartholomew and the Oobleck_, suddenly gets more of this property when you punch or squeeze it. Ketchup does the opposite, losing some of this property when it is shaken, which is why it can suddenly rush out of the bottle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that stays constant for Newtonian fluids such as water, a measure of resistance to flow.

tossups.p: Lava rich in silica has a high value of this property, so it traps gas and tends to erupt explosively, while runny basalt lava flows in rivers on Hawaii. In Earth’s mantle, solid rock with an enormous value of this property slowly flows over millions of years.
tossups.r: Molasses and honey have high values of this property. For 10 points, name this property, a fluid’s resistance to flow.

tossups.p: A popular myth wrongly claims that old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows downward; in fact, glass at room temperature has far too high a value of this property to flow noticeably.
tossups.r: This property usually drops as a liquid is heated. For 10 points, name this property that makes honey and syrup pour slowly.

tossups.p: Dividing this property by a fluid’s density gives a related quantity measured in units called stokes. Water at room temperature has about one centipoise of this property, which equals one-thousandth of a pascal-second.
tossups.r: Honey has thousands of times more of it than water does. For 10 points, name this property, a fluid’s resistance to flow.

tossups.p: When a giant storage tank burst in Boston’s North End in January 1919, cold winter air raised this property of the spilled molasses, making rescue and cleanup much harder. The pascal-second is the SI unit of this property.
tossups.r: Most liquids flow more easily as they warm up because heat lowers this property. For 10 points, name this property that describes how thick and slow-flowing a fluid is.

tossups.p: Ludwig Prandtl [“PRAHN-tul”] showed in 1904 that the effects of this property are concentrated in a thin “boundary layer” of fluid right next to a surface, such as an airplane wing, where the fluid touching the wing does not move relative to it.
tossups.r: Isaac Newton described fluids for which this property stays the same no matter how fast they are stirred. For 10 points, name this property, a fluid’s resistance to flow.

tossups.p: The reciprocal of this property is called fluidity. Glycerin, a thick, sweet liquid whose molecules cling to each other through many hydrogen bonds, has a value of this property more than a thousand times that of water.
tossups.r: Motor oil is rated by it. For 10 points, name this property, which makes honey flow more slowly than water.

Most liquids have less of it when heated, so warm syrup pours faster
Motor oil is graded for it with labels like 10W-30 (the W means winter)

Stokes’ law: the drag on a small sphere equals 6π times this property times the radius times the speed
Measured by timing a steel ball sinking through a tube of liquid

Newtonian fluids like water keep the same value no matter how fast they are stirred
High-silica lava has a lot of it and tends to erupt explosively; basalt lava is runny
It makes a stirred cup of tea eventually stop swirling
Pitch drop experiment at the University of Queensland (begun 1927 by Thomas Parnell): only nine drops fell by 2014
James Clerk Maxwell predicted a gas’s value does not depend on its pressure; gases gain it when heated
Superfluid helium (found by Pyotr Kapitsa and by Allen and Misener, 1937) has none at all
Navier–Stokes equations: deciding whether they always have smooth solutions is a million-dollar Millennium Prize Problem
Poiseuille’s law: flow through a narrow tube depends on the radius to the fourth power divided by it
Robert Millikan used Stokes’ law to find the sizes of his oil drops
Dividing it by a fluid’s density gives a related quantity measured in stokes
Water at room temperature: about 1 centipoise, or one-thousandth of a pascal-second
Myth: old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass flows; really, glass has far too much of it
Boston’s Great Molasses Flood (January 1919): cold air made the spilled molasses thicker, slowing rescue and cleanup
Ludwig Prandtl (1904): its effects are concentrated in a thin boundary layer next to a surface
Its reciprocal is called fluidity
Glycerin’s many hydrogen bonds give it more than a thousand times as much as water
Earth’s solid mantle flows slowly over millions of years because it has an enormous value

trap.title: Thick is not heavy
trap.body: Viscosity is about how slowly a fluid flows, not how heavy it is. Cooking oil is more viscous than water but less dense, so it floats on top of water. Surface tension, the “skin” on a liquid that lets water striders walk on it, is a different property too.
trap.fix: Honey, syrup, motor oil, Stokes’ law, poise, and the pitch drop mean viscosity. Floating, sinking, and mass per volume mean density; water striders, beading droplets, and capillary action mean surface tension.
trap.line: Real answer line: Viscosity (accept dynamic or kinematic viscosity; prompt on thickness or internal friction)
